title: What Is the 'Placebo Effect'
paragraphs: Imagine taking a pill for a headache and feeling better, only to discover later that the pill contained nothing but sugar. This surprising experience is an example of what scientists call the "placebo effect."

A placebo is a treatment that has no active medical ingredient, such as a sugar pill or an injection of salt water. The word "placebo" comes from Latin and means "I shall please." The placebo effect occurs when people's symptoms improve after receiving such a treatment. Scientists now consider it to be a genuine phenomenon, and it has been studied intensively in recent decades.

Researchers believe that the placebo effect is closely connected to people's expectations. In other words, when people believe that a treatment will help them, their brains and bodies may respond in ways that actually reduce their symptoms. Some researchers describe the effect as a response to the whole situation in which a treatment is given, including what patients are told and how they are treated.

The placebo effect plays an important role in medical research. When scientists test a new drug, they usually give some participants the real drug and others a placebo. If the drug works better than the placebo, it suggests that the drug itself is effective, rather than people's expectations.

The placebo effect also has a negative counterpart, known as the "nocebo effect," a term introduced in 1961. This occurs when people experience unpleasant side effects simply because they expect to. For example, some participants who receive a placebo in drug trials report side effects. Researchers believe that the nocebo effect may involve similar processes in the brain to the placebo effect. Interestingly, some research suggests that simply listing possible side effects when patients agree to join a trial may trigger nocebo effects.

Perhaps the most surprising discovery is that placebos may work even when people know they are taking one. These are called "open-label placebos." Early research began with a small study of patients with irritable bowel syndrome, and later studies have tested them for conditions such as chronic back pain and migraines. A 2021 analysis of 11 studies found that open-label placebos had a significant effect. However, research on them is still developing, and scientists do not yet fully understand how they work.
